summary: Providing targeted, quality-assured patient information is essential for informed and autonomous decision-making but remains resource-intensive when delivered face-to-face. Multimedia-supported informed consent may enhance patient understanding and satisfaction while reducing physician time by complementing, rather than replacing, direct interaction. Our PRISMA-based systematic review, aiming to enable clinicians to implement and evaluate such a supplement, identified 907 articles of which 110 reports from OECD countries were included, including 62 randomized controlled trials. Among studies assessing the outcomes of interest, 71% reported improved patient understanding with multimedia tools compared to standard consent, 41% reported increased patient satisfaction (none reported decreases), and 91% found reduced or unchanged patient anxiety. In synthesis, to the extent possible despite substantial heterogeneity, findings suggest benefits and potential efficiency gains, and we were able to derive recommendations. However, considerable methodological variability and limitations affecting internal validity highlight the need for high-quality head-to-head comparative studies to draw more robust conclusions.
